title: Simulating the Evolution of Rock, Paper, Scissors
beats: Blobs compete for food via rock-paper-scissors; rules restated for anyone unfamiliar
Admits RPS food contests are unrealistic, then grounds cycles in side-blotched lizard throat morphs
Winner-take-all rules: winner gets two mangoes and two offspring, tie gives one each
Nine situations collected into a reward table, then named 'matrix' with self-mocking aside
Asks viewer to predict: balance, takeover, or cycling?
Scissors wins, then paper wins on rerun: concludes takeover is random
Bar graph shows only one moment; motivates a plot that shows history
Ternary plot introduced; presenter admits it felt like cheating, builds it from a Cartesian paper-vs-scissors graph
Corners = one strategy wins, edges = two-strategy mixes, interior = all three, outside = impossible
Rotate the y axis 30 degrees to get an equilateral triangle treating strategies equally
Pauses mid-run with rock leading, asks what next; narrates the spiral to extinction
800 trees to smooth randomness; same outward spiral to one survivor
Endless takeover cycle via mutation into the next counter-strategy
Shows the cycle was predictable from the matrix: identical pairings reward switching
Names Nash equilibrium, says jargon is optional, points to previous video
No coexistence yet; two directions: change matrix or allow mixed strategies
Softer payoffs 1.5/0.5 with fractional mangoes as probability; asks predict and why
Same cycling, slower; same matrix structure means same behavior
Adds tie cost; urges viewer to keep predicting rather than let it wash over
Population spirals inward; intuition: majority strategy earns below average
Lizard field study 1990-95 shows an off-center loop; real matrix less symmetric
Mixed strategies: three alleles, 10 combinations, asexual mutation shown on a single blob
One bar per mixture to track population
Original matrix with mixtures: cycles again; brown even-mix bar stands out
Brown is 'aggressively neutral'; refines Nash to weak Nash equilibrium
Predicted browns would take over with tie penalty; confused live on Twitch; whole population balances instead
Four populations from pure starts and pure brown; predict each
Pure strategies cycle; browns resist invaders because mutants suffer tie penalty against themselves; named ESS

metrics.misconception: partial: viewer likely assumes balance or random takeover; presenter's own wrong guess about browns at 12:51
metrics.brute_force: yes 2:12: just run the sim and watch bars before any theory; ternary plot only after bars fail
metrics.examples: ~9 sim conditions; grow by one variable each: pure -> larger -> mutation -> soft payoff -> tie cost -> mixed -> mixed+tie -> special initial conditions
metrics.ending: Lands on ESS name then Patreon; no recap

principles.1: confirmed: 0:00 opens with RPS game everyone knows; 3:17 ternary built from familiar Cartesian graph
principles.2: confirmed: 7:22 Nash labeled optional; 'matrix' named only after table built (1:21)
principles.3: confirmed: ternary plot introduced at 3:01 and reused through every later run until reading it is automatic
principles.4: partly: lizard analogy at 0:30 is real-world grounding, not a bridge to rigor; no formal math ever
principles.5: confirmed: blobs literally eat mangoes and reproduce on screen; mutation shown on one brown blob at 11:11
principles.6: confirmed: 2:12 raw sims with bar graph first; better plot only after bar graph proves inadequate (2:45)
principles.7: confirmed: repeated outward spirals across 5:25, 6:35, 9:06 let viewer see that matrix structure, not magnitude, drives behavior
principles.8: partly: speech steady; slowdown at 3:01-4:37 spends ~95 s on one interface with no new biology
principles.9: confirmed: same spiral/cycle pattern reinforced across matrix variants
principles.10: confirmed: 80 trees -> 800 trees; pure strategies -> 10 mixtures
principles.11: confirmed: mutation added before mixed strategies; Nash before weak Nash before ESS
principles.12: confirmed: lizards (0:30, 10:22), previous teamwork video (7:37), Twitch stream (13:06)
principles.13: partly: says why ternary chosen (history vs one moment, 2:45); tie-cost intuition at 10:05 but explicitly skips calculation

new_moves.name: interface-justified-by-pain
new_moves.what: Use a weak view until its limitation is felt, then introduce the better chart as the cure
new_moves.evidence: 2:45 bar graph only shows one instant -> 3:01 ternary plot

new_moves.name: read-it-off-the-table
new_moves.what: After the sim surprises, show the outcome was readable from the rule table all along
new_moves.evidence: 6:50 identical pairings reward switching; 9:06 same structure, same result

new_moves.name: meta-coaching
new_moves.what: Narrator names the learner's passive drift and asks for continued predictions

new_moves.name: one-variable-ladder
new_moves.what: Each new run changes exactly one knob from the last, so effect is attributable

theory: The video is a controlled experiment ladder: each run changes one knob, the viewer commits to a prediction, and the sim settles it. Theory (matrix structure, Nash, ESS) is introduced only as a post-hoc explanation of something already seen, so vocabulary costs almost nothing. The one heavy interface, the ternary plot, is earned by first showing the bar graph's failure.
velocity: Orchestrator: structure sim lessons as a one-knob-per-step ladder and log which knob changed for the learner model
Voice: insert a predict-pause before every sim run; collect learner commitments and score calibration in evals
Scene builder: start with a lossy chart, let learner feel its limit, then morph it into the better chart (Cartesian -> ternary rotation as an animated transform)
Learner model: name formal terms only after the phenomenon has been observed; flag terms as optional for younger learners
Ghost hands: mid-run pause-and-ask at decision points (rock leads, now what?)
Evals: include a 'presenter-was-wrong' beat where the tutor admits a prior wrong prediction to normalize error
quote: if you continue making predictions, you will learn a bit more
